newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Timor bishop says anti-Indonesian words distorted.
newsitem.headline: Timor bishop says anti-Indonesian words distorted.

text.p: Nobel laureate Bishop Carlos Belo on Wednesday asked a German magazine to apologise for distorting remarks he made during an interview, and denied saying Indonesia had treated East Timorese like "scabby dogs".

In a signed statement detailing his meeting with local government and military officials at his residence in the East Timor capital of Dili last Monday, Belo said he did not intend to tarnish Indonesia in the interview with Der Spiegel.
"I did not intend to tarnish or criticise the Indonesian government, the nation, people or the armed forces," he said.
Belo said he was misquoted in the interview, done in April and published last month after he had won the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize, and denied using the term "scabby dogs."
"I did not know the word scabby. I have just learnt it after the quote was printed," Belo said in the statement, printed on the letterhead of the Dili Apolistic Administrator.
Belo's statement, however, did not refer to the part in the interview where he allegedly said Indonesians had treated East Timorese like "slaves."
Der Spiegel has said it stood by its story.

The publishing of the interview, which received wide coverage in Indonesia, caused an uproar in Jakarta with senior ministers attacking Belo and thousands of members of pro-government youth groups protesting at the national parliament on November 12.

The anti-Belo protests were then met with five consecutive days of demonstrations last week in support of the bishop in East Timor, which climaxed with more than 60,000 people welcoming him when he returned home last Saturday after a meeting in Jakarta.
Belo said there was distortion and manipulation in the Der Spiegel story, adding that he did not say there had been nine assassination attempts on him but only two, in June 1989 and in October 1991.

"Because of the distortions which have been made by Der Spiegel and which have already hurt the feelings of many people, we ask Der Spiegel to apologise to the government of Indonesia and the armed forces," the statement said.
"For the harsh words which have been uttered by the me, I express my heartfelt apologies," it said without elaborating.
Belo, who shared the Nobel Peace Prize last month with East Timor resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta, had maintained a silence on the German report until his Wednesday statement.
He is scheduled to hold a news conference in Dili next week.
Belo was not immediately available for comment on Wednesday.

Indonesia's control of East Timor still faces some political and armed resistance more than 20 years after Jakarta invaded the former Portuguese colony in December 1975 and declared the territory its 27th province the following year.
The United Nations does not recognise Indonesia's sovereignty over East Timor, which it still regards as being administered by Lisbon.
